Rendaku in Japanese: Why Compound Readings Change

Kanjidon Team · Jan 31, 2026

Rendaku, or sequential voicing, is a phonological pattern that can voice the first consonant of the second element in a Japanese compound. It helps explain pairs such as 人（ひと, hito）and 人々（ひとびと, hitobito）. The kanji has not acquired a random new meaning; the pronunciation changes when the word is formed.

The Common Voicing Correspondences

Second element begins withCommon rendaku resultCompound example
kg手 + 紙: て + かみ → てがみ
sz青 + 空: あお + そら → あおぞら
td山 + 寺: やま + てら → やまでら
hb花 + 火: はな + ひ → はなび

These correspondences describe a common outcome, not an instruction to voice every second element. The p-row can appear through consonant doubling and other historical or phonological processes, but h-to-p is not a universal rendaku rule.

Why a One-Line Rule Cannot Predict Every Word

Rendaku interacts with the internal structure of a compound, the origin and lexical identity of its parts, established usage and the sounds inside the second element. Some forms are strongly preferred, some vary and some remain unvoiced. Proper names can be especially difficult because the same written sequence may have more than one conventional reading.

Lyman’s Law Is a Constraint, Not a Complete Algorithm

A well-known generalization says rendaku is commonly blocked when the second element already contains a voiced obstruent. This helps explain many words, but it does not decide every case on its own. Research discusses weak and strong formulations, exceptions and interactions with other factors. Use the constraint to form a hypothesis, not to override an attested pronunciation.

Learn Rendaku at the Word Level

  • Store the full compound with kana or audio, not only the isolated kanji readings.
  • Compare the compound with its second element to notice whether voicing occurred.
  • Check an unfamiliar word in a reliable dictionary, especially for names and specialized terms.
  • Treat variation as lexical information rather than forcing it into a simple exception list.
  • Test the word inside a sentence so pronunciation and meaning stay connected.

A Practical Analysis Workflow

When you meet a new compound, identify the likely component words, predict the unvoiced form, then check the actual dictionary or audio form. If it is voiced, note the correspondence. If it is not, inspect the sounds in the second element and the kind of compound, but keep the verified whole word as the final answer.
